labs.module: Week 4 — SOX / ITGC / SAP Controls Testing
navigation: Re-run or inspect the exact report used in the control test: SUIM, STMS, SM37 or GRC.
Open the same selection criteria/variant and compare to the retained export.
labs.objective: Assess whether SAP-generated reports and screenshots used in testing are complete, accurate, appropriately scoped and reliable for the test purpose.
labs.scenario: Validate selected SUIM/STMS/SM37/GRC evidence before relying on it in a control conclusion.
labs.systems: SAP report/transaction that generated the selected evidence.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify the report name/transaction/app, system/client, extraction date/time and purpose.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Before I rely on any of it, I validate the evidence itself. IPE — Information Produced by the Entity — is where audits quietly break. I took the SUIM user population export from Lab 14 and interrogated it: Source? SUIM, PRD/100, extracted 14:22 on the test date — matches the criteria screenshot. Confirmed: Parameters? No validity exclusions, no user-type filters — matches the documented criteria. Confirmed: Completeness? Count reconciled to an independent license report. Confirmed: Accuracy? I picked three rows at random and traced each back to SU01 — user type, lock status, and role assignment all matched the export. Confirmed: Alteration? The raw file’s timestamp predates any analysis copy, and analysis lives only in the working copy. Confirmed:

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Reconstruct the selection criteria including date range, status, user/role patterns, target system and variants.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: But the STMS import history export had a limitation I documented honestly: it reflects only imports through the transport system — direct production changes made outside STMS would not appear. My control conclusion is scoped accordingly. The principle I wrote in bold: “system generated” does not mean “reliable for every purpose.” Reliability is purpose-specific, and limitations get documented, not hidden.

steps.title: Step 3

navigation: SAP GUI > SUIM > role/user reports for migrated role population.
SAP GUI > PFCG > Display selected ECC/migrated S/4 roles.
GRC > ARA > role/user analysis where available to evaluate resulting risk.
labs.objective: Assess security/control risks created by ECC-to-S/4 role migration and redesign.
labs.scenario: Review migrated/retained roles and identify legacy, broad, obsolete or poorly redesigned access.
labs.systems: SAP GUI; PFCG; SUIM; GRC ARA if available.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Obtain the migrated-role inventory and identify legacy vs redesigned roles.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I pulled the migrated-role inventory from Elena and used SUIM to export current role-to-user assignments for the flagged legacy roles. Raw file, criteria captured. Then PFCG, role by role. The pattern was familiar and ugly: Z:MM:LEGACY-FULL — an ECC-era role with 340 menu entries, retained “temporarily” in S/4, still holding obsolete transactions (ME21, MB52) alongside broad MIGO and MI20 authorizations. Assigned to 23 users. The migration mapping document said it should have been decommissioned in Wave 2. “Temporarily,” Sameer said, “is the most dangerous word in SAP security.”

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Use SUIM to obtain current role/user assignments for selected roles; capture criteria and export.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I ran ARA against the role: it generated 9 risks, several reflecting S/4 process changes the ECC ruleset era never anticipated. The S/4 process redesign had merged steps that ECC kept separate — so old role designs now combined newly incompatible duties. I separated my findings into two buckets, as always: migration governance gaps (no owner review, no UAT evidence, no decommissioning) and technical access risks (obsolete transactions, over-broad values). Remediation priorities ranked: remove legacy access first, redesign second, retest third.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Open selected roles in PFCG Display and review Menu, Authorizations and User assignments.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Key line in the workpaper: a migrated role that technically works can still be dangerously over-privileged, and ECC-era controls don’t automatically survive process redesign. Sameer called Z:MM:LEGACY-FULL “temporary.” I smiled. “Temporary access becomes permanent when nobody owns the exit condition. Show me the Wave 2 decommissioning evidence.” There was none.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Identify obsolete ECC transactions, broad technical/security roles and changed S/4 business functions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L16-MigratedRole-Inventory, Excel file E02-L16-SUIM-LegacyRoleUsers-RAW, Excel file

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Run/review ARA for selected migrated roles/users if GRC is available.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L16-PFCG-LegacyFull, PNG image E04-L16-MigrationMapping-Wave2, PDF file E05-L16-ARA-LegacyRole-Risks, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Compare pre-migration intent to current S/4 access and identify redesign gaps.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The program team argued the role had existed since ECC and therefore represented accepted risk. I documented why migration changed the context: redesigned processes can turn historically separate permissions into new incompatible combinations. Confirmed: current assignments exported

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Document remediation priority and whether access should be removed, redesigned or retested.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: roles inspected in PFCG Confirmed: S/4 process changes considered Confirmed: remediation prioritized

labs.objective: Validate Fiori access end to end: assigned content, launch behavior, backend authorization and troubleshooting evidence.
labs.scenario: Test selected Fiori apps for expected positive and negative access and explain the authorization path.
labs.systems: Fiori Launchpad; PFCG/SUIM; SU53; STAUTHTRACE/ST01 if approved.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Identify app, user, expected business action and expected allow/deny result.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “Tile visibility is not authorization,” I told Elena. “Let’s prove it.” Test case: USER-DCAMPOS should be able to view purchase requisitions in the Fiori app “Manage Purchase Requisitions — Professional” but should not be able to release (approve) them. I confirmed her content assignment in PFCG — the front-end role with the right catalog, and the back-end role carrying the OData authorizations. Then I launched the app as her.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Confirm user-role/content assignment using PFCG/SUIM appropriate to the client architecture.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: She could view PRs. I screenshotted it. Then I attempted the release action. Error. Exactly as designed — negative test passed. Then the reverse test with USER-TNGUYEN, who should be able to release. He launched, executed the release, success. Positive test passed, screenshots captured. But a third case broke: USER-KLEE could see the tile but got a backend error trying to open any PR. Tile visible, app broken — the classic distributed-authorization failure. Immediately after the error, I ran SU53 in the correct ABAP system (front-end versus back-end system confusion is the rookie mistake here). It showed a failed check on authorization object M-EINK-FRG with activity 02 missing from the backend role.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Launch the app and execute the actual business action; do not stop at tile visibility.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I mapped that object back to the PFCG role content and found the backend role had the display authorization but not the release activity — while the catalog assignment suggested full access. The fix direction: align backend role values with intended business action. Trace tools? Not needed — SU53 answered it, and I only trace with approval, scoped tightly, stopped immediately. Elena pointed to the visible tile. “So KLEE has the app.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Capture success or error. If error, run SU53 immediately in the relevant ABAP system.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: “He has the doorway,” I said. “Now we test whether the backend lets him through.” The SU53 failure proved the distinction immediately. I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L17-DCAMPOS-View-OK, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review failed authorization object/field values and map them to PFCG role content.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E02-L17-DCAMPOS-Release-Denied, PNG image E03-L17-TNGUYEN-Release-OK, PNG image

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: If SU53 is insufficient, obtain approval, start STAUTHTRACE/ST01 for the relevant user/time, reproduce once, stop trace promptly and evaluate checks.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E04-L17-KLEE-BackendError, PNG image E05-L17-SU53-MEINKFRG, PNG image E06-L17-PFCG-BackendRole, PNG image

steps.action: Perform the required negative test with an unauthorized user/role where the lab case provides one.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The reviewer asked why I did not launch a trace. I documented proportionality: SU53 identified the failed object, so broader tracing was unnecessary. Use the least invasive diagnostic that answers the question. Confirmed: actual business action tested Confirmed: not just tiles

steps.title: Step 8
steps.action: Conclude whether Fiori and backend authorization align with intended access.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: positive and negative cases both Confirmed: SU53 used correctly in the right system Confirmed: role source identified

labs.objective: Identify privileged users/roles/profiles and determine whether access is restricted, justified, monitored and segregated.
labs.scenario: Assess high-privilege access including SAP_ALL/SAP_NEW, security administration, Basis/technical access and other critical authorizations.
labs.systems: SUIM; SU01; PFCG; GRC ARA/EAM where applicable.

steps.title: Define the privileged-access criteria for the lab
steps.action: Define the privileged-access criteria for the lab: profiles, roles, critical transactions/authorization objects.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I defined privilege explicitly before hunting it — because “admin” labels lie. My criteria: SAP-ALL/SAP-NEW profiles, security administration roles (S-USER-* objects with change activity), Basis/technical roles with production transport capability, and critical objects like S-TABU-NAM with broad table access. SUIM by profile: 6 users with SAP-ALL. Raw export saved. SU01 on the first: USER-ADMIN01 — a dialog account, interactive use, SAP-ALL with no expiry. Justification on file? None. Owner? Listed as “IT.” Monitoring? None found.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Run SUIM report(s) that identify the relevant population. Capture criteria and export raw results.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The second one was worse: USER-DEV03, a developer, holding a role with production import authorization in STMS. Development plus production change capability in one pair of hands. I opened the role in PFCG and screenshotted the S-TRANSPRT object with activity 6 (import) against production — that’s the smoking gun, the value, and the role, all in one frame. Third pattern: a generic privileged ID, RFC-SUPER, no named owner, used by three interfaces. Standing privilege where emergency access should be the model — and no periodic review evidence anywhere.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Select privileged users and inspect SU01 status/roles/profiles.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena’s team produced justification for two of the six; the rest had nothing. My finding: privileged access was not restricted, justified, or monitored to standard, with remediation split by pattern — emergency-only access via EAM for the standing privileges, removal for the rest, and a hard rule that developers never hold production import rights. “This role isn’t called administrator,” the owner said. “I’m not auditing names,” I replied. “I’m auditing capability.” The S-TRANSPRT activity value told the story more clearly than the role title ever could.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Open the source role in PFCG and identify the critical authorization that creates privilege.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L18-SAPALL-Population-RAW, Excel file E02-L18-ADMIN01-SU01, PNG image

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Review business/technical justification, ownership and monitoring evidence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L18-DEV03-STRANSPRT, PNG image E04-L18-RFC-SUPER-Ownership, Excel file E05-L18-PrivilegedAccess-Assessment, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: If privilege is emergency-only, reconcile to EAM rather than accepting standing access without explanation.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Management produced justification for only two of six SAP-ALL users. I did not treat missing paperwork as the only issue; I also tested ownership, expiry, monitoring, and whether standing privilege should be replaced by controlled emergency access. Confirmed: privilege criteria documented

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Identify inappropriate combinations such as security administration plus business processing or development plus production change capability.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: population exported Confirmed: users traced to source role/object Confirmed: justification and monitoring tested

labs.lab: Lab 19 — Independent QA/QC of Tester Workpapers
navigation: For each tester workpaper, return to the exact SAP transaction/report named in that workpaper.
Re-run or inspect the relevant population/detail using the same criteria, then independently assess the result.
labs.objective: Independently reperform key tester procedures and determine whether tester conclusions are supported by complete, accurate evidence.
labs.scenario: Review the capstone tester workpapers and identify missed exceptions, incomplete populations and unsupported conclusions.
labs.systems: Use the SAP source corresponding to each tester workpaper: SUIM/GRC/STMS/SM37/ARM/EAM as applicable.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Select the tester workpaper and identify control objective, population, sample and conclusion.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I took the UAR workpaper first. Population stated: 412 users. The retained raw export: 411 rows. One row missing. I re-ran the SUIM criteria myself — 412. The tester had exported after applying a filter. An incomplete population invalidates a clean-sample conclusion, and I wrote exactly that in the QA note. Next: the change-management workpaper concluded “operating effectively.” I re-ran STMS for the same period and opened the transport the tester had sampled. Then I opened the one next to it — which the tester hadn’t sampled — and found it was the developer’s own production import, ticket unapproved. The tester missed it because the sample never touched it; but the workpaper’s population was also under-counted (67 transports tested against a stated population of 61 — the criteria screenshot showed a date range that cut six transports off).

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Check whether the tester retained selection criteria and raw population.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Third: the EAM workpaper — controller review accepted at face value. I reperformed: the controller review for the session in question was dated, but the activity log attached to the review showed unexplained SE16 usage that the review comment didn’t address. Missed exception. Each workpaper got a QA note: issue, evidence, impact, required correction. Ratings: revise, revise, fail. I preserved the original tester evidence untouched — read-only, always — and saved my re-performance evidence with QA prefixes. The principle, written in the log header: QA/QC is independent verification, not making the tester’s work pass.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Reperform the critical SAP step using the same source.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The junior consultant said, “The conclusion is right; I just need help cleaning up the workpaper.” “My job is not to make it look right,” I said. “My job is to determine whether another reviewer can reach the same conclusion from the retained evidence.”

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Compare tester evidence to SAP source and look for contradictory facts or omitted exceptions.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: QA01-L19-UAR-Reperformance.xlsx QA02-L19-STMS-Reperformance.xlsx

steps.title: Step 5
steps.action: Verify sample items and reviewer notes.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: QA03-L19-EAM-Reperformance.xlsx QA04-L19-Review-Log.xlsx

steps.title: Document QA review note
steps.action: Document QA review note: issue, evidence, impact and required correction.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Three QA results—revise, revise, fail—were tied to concrete defects: incomplete population, truncated transport period, and superficial EAM review. Each note stated issue, evidence, impact, and required correction. Confirmed: Conclusion is evidence-linked Confirmed: Raw evidence is preserved

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Do not edit the original tester evidence; record QA in the QA/QC review log.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: Reviewer can reproduce the result Confirmed: Open questions and limitations are documented

labs.objective: Evaluate identified SAP control exceptions for risk, severity, root cause, scope and reporting impact.
labs.scenario: Assess capstone deficiencies including termination, privileged population, change segregation, Firefighter purpose, weak mitigation and Fiori backend access.
labs.systems: SAP/GRC source relevant to each deficiency; evidence already obtained in prior capstone testing may be reperformed as needed.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Take one deficiency at a time and identify the failed criterion/control.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Now I took each exception and built a defensible deficiency. I started with the termination finding from Lab 2. Back to SUIM/SU01 — condition confirmed, evidence ID attached. Scope: was it one user or systemic? I re-ran the reconciliation of terminated employees against active SAP users: 11 of 43 terminations in the period still had valid access. Not isolated — systemic. Root cause: no automated deprovisioning trigger from HR; removal depended on a manual ticket nobody owned. Effect: ex-employees retained production access for weeks. Compensating controls asserted? A monthly review — but I tested it in Lab 13 and found its population excluded locked users, so it demonstrably didn’t catch these. Severity: significant deficiency, per the methodology criteria, because the control absence was systemic and the compensating control was ineffective.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Return to the SAP/GRC source and confirm the condition is factual and evidence-supported.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: The privileged-access finding: likelihood high, impact high, but scope smaller (6 users, now being remediated). Severity: high finding, not a significant deficiency. The Firefighter controller-review finding: I was careful — do not overstate. The emergency access itself was approved; the monitoring failed. Root cause: controller reviews treated as perfunctory sign-off, no criteria, no SLA. Management action: define review criteria, 48-hour review SLA, retraining. I wrote every one in the full structure: Criteria, then Condition, then Cause, then Effect/Risk, then Evidence, then Recommendation. And I flagged the trap explicitly in my notes: do not downgrade severity because management plans to fix it later, and do not upgrade it beyond what the evidence shows.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Determine affected population/time period and whether the issue is isolated or systemic.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena asked, “Can we call the terminated-user issue isolated? We only found one in the original sample.” “Not until we scope it,” I said. The reconciliation found 11 of 43 terminations with valid access. The evidence changed the story from one bad account to a process failure.

steps.title: Step 4
steps.action: Assess likelihood/impact in the context of the control objective.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was: E01-L20-Termination-Reconciliation, Excel file E02-L20-PrivilegedFinding-Assessment, Excel file

steps.title: Identify root cause
steps.action: Identify root cause: design, execution, evidence, configuration, governance or monitoring.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: E03-L20-EAM-Deficiency-Assessment, Excel file W05-L20-Deficiency-Register, Excel file

steps.title: Step 6
steps.action: Consider compensating controls only if evidenced.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: I challenged my own conclusions in both directions: do not minimize a systemic absence of control, and do not overstate a monitoring failure when the underlying emergency access was properly approved. Confirmed: conditions reconfirmed Confirmed: scope assessed

steps.title: Step 7
steps.action: Assign lab severity/classification and recommended management action.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Confirmed: root causes identified Confirmed: severity rationale documented

labs.objective: Validate whether management’s claimed remediation actually resolves the SAP control deficiency and is operating as intended.
labs.scenario: Retest remediation claims and classify them as closed, partially remediated, risk accepted or still open.
labs.systems: SAP/GRC source corresponding to each remediated deficiency.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Read the original deficiency and management remediation claim.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena’s team came back with remediation claims. My job: verify, not trust. Claim 1: “Terminated user access removed — ticket closed.” I went to SU01. USER-RSHARMA: locked, but the role assignments were still present, and the validity date was unchanged. Locked is not removed. Ticket said closed; the condition persisted. Classification: still open. The ticket was administrative closure, not remediation. Claim 2: “SoD conflict in Z:MM:PURCHASER redesigned.” I opened PFCG — MIGO removed from authorizations. Then I ran ARA on the role: conflict count dropped from 9 to 2. The 2 remaining were different risks than the original — I traced them and found they predated the change and weren’t part of this remediation’s scope. Classification: validated closed — for the specific condition. I documented that closure was scoped to the finding, not a claim that the role is now risk-free.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.action: Identify the exact condition that must change for closure.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Claim 3: “Firefighter review process strengthened — policy updated.” I asked for operating evidence. They produced the new policy document — and nothing else. No review performed under the new criteria since implementation. Classification: partial — design changed, operation not yet evidenced. Follow-up date set. Claim 4: One item was labeled “remediated” but the evidence was a signed risk-acceptance form. I reclassified it honestly: risk accepted, which is a governance decision, not technical remediation, and must never be reported as “closed/remediated.” Before closing each item I asked: does the fix address the root cause and the full population, or just the one user in the finding? For Claim 1, the systemic fix (HR-triggered deprovisioning) was still in build — so I logged residual risk and a follow-up validation date.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.action: Return to the relevant SAP/GRC source and obtain current-state evidence.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Elena pointed to the closed ticket. “RSHARMA is fixed.” I opened SU01. “Locked, yes. Roles still assigned, validity unchanged. The ticket is closed; the condition is not.” I indexed the evidence before writing the conclusion. My training-file convention for this lab was:

steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

steps.action: For role/ruleset changes, rerun risk analysis or inspect updated role content as appropriate.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.

labs.objective: Convert the completed SAP controls testing into an audit-ready evidence package, executive dashboard and management report.
labs.scenario: Prepare the final capstone reporting package for ABC Manufacturing using only conclusions supported by indexed evidence.
labs.systems: No new transaction is mandatory; return to SUIM/PFCG/GRC/STMS/SM37/Fiori only to resolve evidence gaps identified during final QA.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.action: Reconcile all planned capstone deliverables to completed workpapers.
steps.confirm: Confirm this step is complete and retain the required evidence before continuing.
steps.narration: Final week. No new transactions — my job now was to make the whole engagement survive an independent reviewer’s eyes. I started with the evidence index. Every file checked: named correctly, opens, criteria visible, cross-references intact. I found one broken reference — a finding cited E03 but the file was labeled E04 — and fixed the index, not the evidence. Then the findings register: every finding had criteria, condition, risk, cause, recommendation, owner, status, and evidence ID. One finding had no evidence ID attached. It went back to its source, evidence re-extracted as new dated evidence, index updated. No exceptions.

steps.title: Step 2
